query: For a selected high-entropy alloy whose superconducting behavior remains uncharacterized, what governs whether and how superconductivity emerges in the low-temperature test regime, and why? Propose one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison with the starting state, the observations expected relative to that baseline, the limits over which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Application of moderate hydrostatic pressure will enhance the superconducting Tc by modifying interatomic distances and electron–phonon coupling in the HEA.
generation.material_initial_state: A pristine, bcc-structured HEA with a baseline Tc measured at ambient pressure.
generation.intervention: Subject the sample to incrementally increasing hydrostatic pressures up to approximately 20 GPa using a diamond-anvil cell.
generation.conditions: Low-temperature (<10 K) superconductivity measurements under controlled high-pressure conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Pressure-induced reduction in interatomic spacing enhances electron overlap and may modify phonon spectra without inducing a structural phase transition.
generation.mechanism: The increased pressure tunes the electron–phonon coupling by altering the lattice dynamics and density-of-states near the Fermi level, thereby increasing Tc modestly.
generation.predicted_outcome: Tc is expected to increase by roughly 1–2 K from its ambient-pressure value within the 0–20 GPa range, after which it may plateau or decrease.
generation.baseline: The superconducting transition temperature measured at ambient pressure.
generation.boundary: The effect is valid only within a pressure regime where the bcc structure remains invariant (approximately up to 20 GPa), avoiding structural phase transitions.
generation.uncertainty: Pressure-induced changes can be sensitive to experimental uniformity; uncertainties arise in the exact pressure dependence and potential secondary effects.

measurements: Superconducting Tc values at controlled pressures

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the evolution of Tc does not show the predicted modest increase (approximately 1–2 K) within the specified pressure range, or if a phase change is detected, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Pressure is one of the variables that can uncover unexpected phenomena and properties (). For superconductors in particular, the pressure-induced enhancement of critical transition temperatures in copper-oxide and iron-pnictide superconductors (), the reemergence of superconductivity in the alkaline iron selenide () and heavy fermion superconductors (), pressure-induced superconductivity in H3S () and elements (, ), are examples. Therefore, looking for new phenomena in the superconducting HEA under pressure is of great interest. Here we report high-pressure studies on the superconducting HEA (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33, which has a critical transition temperature to the superconducting state (TC) of about 7.8 K at ambient pressure (, ). Our observations demonstrate that this alloy exhibits extraordinarily robust superconductivity––its zero-resistance superconducting state is still achieved even at a pressure of 190.6 GPa, or almost 2 megabars (1 Mbar = 1011 pascal), a pressure like that within the outer core of the earth. Such a superconductor with a highly robust zero-resistance state, existing continuously from 1 atm to geological pressures, is extremely unusual and is in fact unique

Consistent results are obtained from another sample in the pressure range of 0.3–30.1 GPa, as shown in Fig. 3. To investigate the superconducting behavior at higher pressures, we carried out resistance measurements for the third sample over the wide pressure range of 1.5–179.2 GPa (Fig. 2 C and D). As shown in Fig. 2C, the superconducting state still survives at a pressure as high as 179.2 GPa. Surprisingly, the zero-resistance state still exists at this high pressure (Fig. 2D). The magnetic field dependence of the superconducting transition measured at 103.7 and 179.2 GPa, respectively, further confirms the superconducting nature (Fig. 2 E and F). Furthermore, our measurements up to 190.6 GPa on the fourth sample show the reproducibility of the results (Fig. 3). This is an unusual behavior of such robust zero-resistance superconductivity in a material from 1 atm up to near 2 Mbar, a pressure found inside the outer core of the earth. Pressure–Temperature Phase Diagram.

We have studied the crystal and electronic structure and the robustness of superconducting states in a HEA-type metal telluride (MTe; M = Ag, In, Sn, Pb, Bi) under high pressure using a polycrystalline sample, and the results were compared with the pressure effects for a middle-entropy system (AgPbBiTe3) and a reference system of PbTe. PbTe exhibits a structural transition from a NaCl-type to an orthorhombic Pnma structure at low pressures, and further transitions to a CsCl-type structure at high pressures. When the superconductivity of the CsCl-type PbTe is observed, it is found that its superconducting transition temperature (Tc) decreases with pressure. In contrast, in HEA-type AgInSnPbBiTe5, Tc is almost independent of pressure, for pressures ranging from 13.0 to 35.1 GPa. In addition, the middle-entropy system, AgPbBiTe3, shows a slight decrease in Tc with pressure in the CsCl-type structure, which is intermediate trend between PbTe and AgInSnPbBiTe5. Those results suggest that the robustness of superconductivity to external pressure has been enhanced by the increase in configurational entropy of mixing at the metal (M) site in MTe. papers.title: Superconductivity in a uranium containing high entropy alloy.
papers.approach: Experimental heat capacity, resistivity, and magnetic measurements on alloys with uranium substitution.
papers.findings: The superconducting transition temperature (Tc) is lower than in Zr analogues, and the heat capacity data supports a broadened and weakened superconducting transition. The presence of uranium ions appears to reduce Tc and Hc2 relative to expectations.
papers.mechanism: The proposed mechanisms include pair breaking due to uranium ions, potential modifications of the effective electron count via intermediate valence behavior, and increased disorder effects when an f-element replaces a d-element.

papers.title: Growth and Characterization of ROBiS2 High-Entropy Superconducting Single Crystals.
papers.system: ROBiS2 (where RO is a mix of rare-earth elements)
papers.approach: Synthesis of single crystals followed by resistivity and magnetic field anisotropy measurements to probe Tc, ΔSmix effects, and carrier concentration via transport studies.
papers.findings: Despite similar amounts of Ce4+ among samples, the sample with the highest mixing entropy (ΔSmix) showed lower Tc and lower superconducting anisotropy, suggesting that high ΔSmix may reduce carrier concentration and alter local structures.
papers.mechanism: Two possible mechanisms were proposed: reduced carrier concentration due to diminished charge transfer and a high-entropy effect altering local structures, both of which can suppress Tc.

papers.title: Evidence for isotropic s-wave superconductivity in high-entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Magnetic penetration-depth and critical field measurements; analysis based on the BCS model in the dirty limit.
papers.findings: Both alloy compositions show isotropic s-wave superconductivity consistent with weak-coupling BCS theory; the measured temperature dependence of λ and Hc1/Hc2 data support a conventional single-gap behavior.
papers.mechanism: Superconductivity is governed by conventional phonon-mediated pairing in the dirty limit, where atomic-scale disorder is high, yet the pairing remains isotropic. Orbital effects rather than pure disorder control the upper critical field.

papers.title: The Effect of Scandium on the Structure, Microstructure and Superconductivity of Equimolar Sc-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Refractory High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.approach: Synthesis via arc-melting followed by structural characterization (XRD, microscopy) and superconducting measurements (electrical resistivity, specific heat, Meissner effect).
papers.findings: Addition of scandium leads to a two-phase microstructure (bcc and hcp) with superconductivity arising solely from the bcc phase, which retains parameters similar to the parent Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy.
papers.mechanism: Superconductivity is attributed to the bcc phase that fits conventional BCS behavior, while scandium acts to increase chemical complexity without altering the superconducting state of the bcc matrix.

papers.title: Enhanced Superconducting Critical Parameters in a New High-Entropy Alloy Nb0.34Ti0.33Zr0.14Ta0.11Hf0.08
papers.approach: Combined experimental measurements (resistivity, specific heat) and electronic structure calculations (KKR-CPA) to extract superconducting parameters and thermodynamic properties.
papers.findings: The alloy exhibits type-II superconductivity near 7.5 K with a high upper critical field and properties consistent with intermediate electron–phonon coupling in the BCS framework.
papers.mechanism: Superconductivity is mediated by phonons with electron–phonon coupling in a disordered, bcc lattice. Disorder and density-of-states effects from the specific composition are key in setting Tc and Hc2.

papers.title: Robust zero resistance in a superconducting high-entropy alloy at pressures up to 190 GPa.
papers.approach: High-pressure electrical resistance and magnetic measurements up to 190 GPa to evaluate the persistence and evolution of superconductivity.
papers.findings: Zero-resistance superconductivity is maintained from ambient pressure up to nearly 190 GPa, with Tc modestly increasing then slightly decreasing with pressure. The robustness is attributed to the stability of the bcc structure and the resilience of its electronic structure under compression.
papers.mechanism: The mechanism revolves around the stable crystallographic structure and disorder-tolerant electronic states. Orbital limiting and potential strong spin-orbit coupling may play roles in setting the pressure evolution of Tc.

papers.title: Robustness of superconductivity to external pressure in high-entropy-alloy-type metal telluride AgInSnPbBiTe5.
papers.approach: High-pressure studies combining structural and electronic spectral measurements on polycrystalline samples to probe Tc evolution.
papers.findings: Tc in the HEA telluride is nearly independent of pressure over a wide range compared to middle-entropy systems and PbTe, suggesting that enhanced configurational entropy reinforces superconducting robustness under external pressure.
papers.mechanism: The high configurational entropy of mixing (ΔSmix) is proposed to stabilize the superconducting phase against pressure-induced changes, likely through its effects on the crystal and electronic structure.

established: HEAs can crystallize in simple structures (typically bcc) despite high compositional disorder and support conventional BCS-type superconductivity.
Superconducting properties in HEAs are sensitive to electron count, disorder, and mixing entropy, with evidence that both enhanced disorder and controlled crystallinity play roles in Tc.
Conventional s-wave (BCS) superconductivity is often observed in HEAs despite the atomic-scale disorder.
High-pressure studies demonstrate that some HEAs maintain robust superconductivity even under extreme compressive conditions.

approaches_tried.approach: Elemental substitution (e.g., introducing uranium or scandium) to modify electron count and disorder.
approaches_tried.outcome: Uranium incorporation weakens superconductivity (lower Tc and Hc2) likely via pair breaking and intermediate valence effects, while scandium addition leads to a two-phase structure where superconductivity is preserved in the bcc phase.

approaches_tried.approach: Systematic variation of mixing entropy (ΔSmix) through compositional tuning (e.g., ROBiS2 crystals, metal telluride HEAs).
approaches_tried.outcome: High ΔSmix can reduce Tc and alter superconducting anisotropy, though in some systems (e.g., AgInSnPbBiTe5) it enhances superconductivity robustness to pressure.

approaches_tried.approach: High-pressure experiments to examine the evolution of superconductivity.
approaches_tried.outcome: Superconductivity persists over a wide pressure range with moderate Tc variations, underscoring the role of a stable bcc structure and robust electronic states.

mechanisms: Phonon-mediated (BCS) pairing in the dirty limit, where disorder is present but superconductivity remains isotropic.
Effect of disorder and mixing entropy on electron count and local structure, which in turn affect the electron–phonon coupling strength and Tc.
Orbital limiting effects and spin-orbit coupling contributions in determining the upper critical field, especially under high pressure.
disagreements: The role of high mixing entropy (ΔSmix) appears to be system dependent: in some cases it correlates with a suppression of Tc (as seen in ROBiS2 crystals), while in others it appears to enhance robustness against external perturbations (as in AgInSnPbBiTe5).
There is a debate whether the observed Tc variations are primarily driven by changes in carrier concentration or by disorder-induced modifications of the superconducting state.
open_questions: In a HEA with uncharacterized superconducting behavior, how do variations in electron count versus atomic-scale disorder specifically govern the emergence and magnitude of superconductivity at low temperatures?
What is the quantitative interplay between configurational entropy, local structural heterogeneity, and electron–phonon coupling in defining the superconducting parameters?
How do mechanisms such as orbital limiting and spin–orbit effects compete or cooperate with disorder effects in setting the critical fields and Tc across different HEA systems?
opportunities: Conduct controlled experiments on a selected, uncharacterized HEA by systematically varying its chemical composition to span a range of mixing entropies while keeping the overall crystal structure constant.

Combine spectroscopic techniques (e.g., X-ray absorption spectroscopy, scanning tunneling microscopy) with transport measurements to assess the role of local electronic structure and disorder on superconductivity.

Undertake a controlled comparison between the pristine (starting) state and modified alloys (e.g., by doping non-magnetic elements) to test hypotheses regarding the influence of carrier concentration and disorder on superconducting emergence.

Explore the pressure dependence of Tc in such HEAs to delineate the limits over which conventional BCS behavior holds versus regimes where other effects (e.g., orbital limitations, spin–orbit interactions) become dominant.

directions.direction: Tuning electron count via compositional substitution
directions.assessment: Directly targets the effective electron density and electron–phonon coupling which are known to influence Tc in HEAs. Supported by multiple studies (e.g., PMC7070041, PMC7364703) and is experimentally feasible by minor alloying substitutions.

Addresses the role of atomic-scale disorder on superconductivity. Prior evidence (PMC8838456) indicates that increased crystallinity is positively correlated with superconducting strength. This intervention is controllable and directly tests disorder-mediated pair breaking.

directions.direction: Introducing controlled magnetic impurities to induce pair breaking
directions.assessment: Tests the sensitivity of the superconducting state to magnetic pair breaking, as suggested by the uranium-doping case (PMC7070041). It directly probes the mechanism by which local moments may disrupt Cooper pairing.

directions.direction: Modulating interatomic distances via applied pressure
directions.assessment: Leverages high-pressure experiments to modify the electron overlap and phonon spectra without changing the chemistry or structure in a significant way. Prior studies (PMC5740615) show pressure effects on Tc, and this approach is feasible within controlled pressure ranges.

directions.direction: Direct in situ characterization of local electronic structure (e.g., tunneling spectroscopy)
directions.assessment: Aims to probe the density-of-states and pairing symmetry directly, linking local electronic structure to superconducting properties. While informative, the technique requires more complex instrumentation and may not directly isolate the governing mechanism relative to compositional or processing changes.

candidates.hypothesis: Altering the effective electron count via minor substitution will modulate the superconducting Tc in the HEA.
candidates.intervention: Substitute approximately 5% of a key d-metal (e.g., replace Nb with a lower-valence non-magnetic element such as V) to decrease the effective electron count.

candidates.hypothesis: Post-synthesis annealing to enhance crystallinity will sharpen the superconducting transition and modestly increase Tc in the HEA.
candidates.intervention: Anneal the alloy at approximately 800°C under an inert atmosphere for a controlled duration to increase crystallinity without phase segregation.

candidates.hypothesis: Introducing a low concentration of magnetic impurities will suppress superconductivity via pair-breaking effects in the HEA.
candidates.intervention: Dope the HEA with a small amount (approximately 2–3%) of a magnetic element (e.g., uranium) that is known to introduce local moments.
